title: Nettles
hookLine: Milarepa lives on nettles in a cave until his skin turns green, singing songs

cards: A thief creeps into a mountain cave at night, feeling along the walls for anything worth taking. In the dark, a voice starts laughing.

It's the man who lives there, Milarepa, and he says something like: you're looking by night for what I can't find in the daytime. The thief finds nothing, because there is nothing. A cooking pot, perhaps.
Some wild greens. Marpa has given Milarepa the teaching and sent him to the mountains to practice, and Milarepa has taken him at his word.

teach.b: In his life story, Milarepa sits in caves far from any village, and the one thing growing near his door is nettles.
He boils them and eats them, day after day, until, the story says, his body grows thin and his skin turns green. When people come by, some take him for a ghost.
This isn't poverty he can't escape. It's simplicity he chose, so that nothing would pull him away from practice. Food was fuel, and nettles would do.
Here's the surprise: Milarepa wasn't grim and silent in that cave.
He sang. When hunters, his sister, old friends or skeptical scholars turned up, he answered them in songs, about impermanence, about his teacher's kindness, about the joy of the mountains.
His songs are still sung and studied.

teach.h: THIN AS A GHOST, FULL OF SONG.
teach.b: So two pictures sit side by side: a man so thin he looks like a ghost, and a man so full he can't stop singing. The story doesn't treat that as a contradiction.
Owning less made room for something. In the Life, this is the calling Marpa sent him to, one man's road after a hard training, not a menu for anyone else.
What it offers is smaller: a meal that's just a meal, enough without the extra, and space left over for a song.

how: Tibetan paintings can show Milarepa with green-tinged skin and a hand cupped to his ear as he sings, and his songs are recited and studied in Kagyu communities and beyond.

o: the thorny hedge around Marpa's farm
the wild greens Milarepa lived on in his cave
the thorns Marpa put in Milarepa's bed

s: Milarepa lived silently in his cave
he sang, answering visitors with songs.
the story says his skin turned green from nettles
he ate them so long that his body grew thin and green.
some visitors took the thin, green Milarepa for a ghost
the story says his body grew so thin and green that people were startled.

games.q: you're Milarepa. a thief is feeling around your cave in the dark. what do you do?
o: laugh, and tell him he won't find anything.
games.why: Milarepa laughed: the thief was searching by night for what he couldn't find by day.

practice: Notice how little you need for these few minutes: a place to sit, air, a body that breathes, and let everything else wait outside the cave.
With each out-breath, gently set down one want, a snack, a message, a plan, and see what's left.

wordCard.voice: Nettles. The wild greens Milarepa lived on in his cave, until, the story says, his skin turned green, while he sang. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: green from nettles. Thin as a ghost, and still singing in the cave. Till tomorrow.

sources.ref: The Life of Milarepa (Tsangnyön Heruka), the years in the caves
